opus-5.5.text:
I think the bar is actually quite simple to state, even if it's hard to meet: a demo should tell you honestly what the robot can do *on its own, repeatedly, in conditions it hasn't been tuned for*. Right now a lot of videos fail on at least one of those three.

First, **autonomy disclosure**. If there's teleoperation anywhere in the clip, even a partial correction, it should be labeled clearly on screen, not buried in a footnote. Teleoperation is a legitimate tool for collecting data, and there's nothing shameful about it. But when a teleoperated video circulates as if it shows autonomous capability, it misleads the public and investors, and in the end it hurts the whole field's credibility.

Second, **success rate, not best take**. A single beautiful take tells you almost nothing. If you ran the task fifty times and it worked thirty-eight, say so. Better yet, show the failures. Honestly, the failure cases often tell you more about where the technology really stands than the successes do.

Third, **generalization**. Is this the same table, the same lighting, the same cup in the same spot as during training? Or did you move to a new room, swap in objects the model has never seen, and let someone perturb the scene? A robot folding one specific towel in one specific lab is a very different claim from a robot handling arbitrary laundry in a stranger's home. The demo should state which one it is.

And fourth, I'd add **speed and continuity**. If the video is played at 4x or 8x, or stitched from multiple cuts, that needs to be marked. Real-time, single-shot, uncut footage is much harder to fake and much more informative.

Ideally, the field moves toward third-party evaluation: standardized tasks, unseen environments, someone outside your company setting up the scene. That's how computer vision and NLP earned trust with benchmarks, and embodied AI needs its own version. It's harder for robotics because the physical world doesn't fit neatly into a dataset, but I think it's necessary. Otherwise we risk a hype cycle where expectations run far ahead of reality, and when the gap shows up, everyone pays for it, including the teams doing honest work.

r001.rationale: The response permits teleoperation as a legitimate tool when clearly labeled; it does not say credible demonstrations must exclude it.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes labeled teleoperation from footage presented as autonomous, explaining that concealed teleoperation misleads viewers.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the simplest standard is this: a demo should show the robot doing something it has never been rehearsed on, in front of people who can poke at it.

Right now a lot of public demos are what I'd call "performance" rather than "evidence." You see a humanoid folding a shirt beautifully, and you don't know whether that's the hundredth take, whether the shirt is the exact one from the training set, whether someone is teleoperating behind the curtain, or whether the lighting and table height were tuned for weeks. Any one of those turns a research result into a video.

So the first requirement is honesty about the setup. Is it autonomous or teleoperated? What fraction is scripted? Say it on screen. Teleoperation is not shameful, it's how we collect data, but it shouldn't be dressed up as autonomy.

The second is generalization on the spot. Let the audience bring an object the team hasn't seen. Change the position, change the background, hand the robot a cup instead of a bottle. If the policy only works on a fixed scene, that's a very different claim from "the robot can grasp things."

The third is failure rate. A single success tells you almost nothing. I'd rather see twenty consecutive attempts with the number of failures reported than one flawless clip. Honestly, a demo with two visible failures out of twenty is more convincing to me than a perfect one, because it looks like reality.

And finally, speed. Many demos are heavily sped up. Real-time, continuous, uncut footage should be the default, and if it's edited, say so.

I'd put it this way: we in the field have gotten good at making robots look capable. The harder and more valuable thing is making them actually capable, and the standard for demos should make the two indistinguishable, so that people can trust what they see.

r001.rationale: The response allows teleoperation when it is disclosed, so it does not say demonstrations should exclude it.

r002.rationale: It says teams should state on screen whether a demo is autonomous or teleoperated, and says teleoperation should not be presented as autonomy.

astra-6.text:
I think the basic standard is that the audience should be able to understand what the robot did, under what conditions, and how much human help it needed. Was it autonomous, remotely controlled, or following a scripted sequence? Those can all be useful demonstrations, but they support very different claims.

Then there’s repeatability. One successful attempt shows that something is possible; it doesn’t tell you how reliably the robot can do it. If you show ten attempts, including the failures, people can make a much better judgment. And if you’re claiming the robot can generalize, you should vary the objects or the environment rather than repeat exactly the same setup.

For me, a credible demonstration doesn’t have to be flawless. It has to make the limits visible. A modest capability demonstrated honestly is much more convincing than a spectacular clip whose conditions nobody understands.

r001.rationale: The response says remotely controlled demonstrations can be useful, so it does not require excluding teleoperation.

r002.rationale: It says the audience should know whether the robot was remotely controlled and that this supports a different claim, distinguishing disclosed control from an unexplained demonstration.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the standard should be that the audience can tell what the robot actually did, under what conditions, and how reliably it can do it again. Was it autonomous, teleoperated, or following a scripted sequence? What was known in advance? If a person intervened, that should be disclosed.

Then we should look beyond a successful clip. Can it repeat the task across multiple trials, with some variation in the objects or environment? How often does it fail, and what happens when it fails? A demonstration doesn’t have to show a robot that can do everything. A narrow capability can be impressive, as long as the claim matches the evidence.

r001.rationale: The response asks whether a demonstration was autonomous, teleoperated, or scripted and says interventions should be disclosed; it does not say teleoperation must be excluded.

r002.rationale: It calls for disclosure of teleoperation or human intervention, but does not distinguish openly disclosed teleoperation from teleoperation concealed from the audience.
